units.t: Planet Earth & Climate. Episode three.
In this episode: Ice ages, Glaciers: rivers of ice and When the Sahara was green.
Part one. Ice ages.
Twenty thousand years ago you could have walked from Melbourne to Hobart, and on to New Guinea.
The reason lies in a slow wobble in Earth's orbit.
Still in an ice age.
To geologists, an ice age is any long period when large ice sheets exist on Earth.
By that definition we are living in one now, because Antarctica and Greenland are covered in ice.
The current ice age began about 2.
6 million years ago.
Within it, the climate has swung between cold glacial periods, when ice sheets spread across North America and northern Europe, and shorter warm interglacial periods like today's.
Our interglacial, the Holocene, began about 11,700 years ago.
When people say 'the Ice Age', they usually mean the most recent glacial period, which peaked around 20,000 years ago.
Milankovitch cycles.
Serbian scientist Milutin Milanković calculated how small orbital changes alter the sunlight reaching different latitudes.
Eccentricity, the shape of Earth's orbit, varies over about 100,000 years.
Obliquity, the axis tilt, varies between about 22 and 24.
5 degrees over 41,000 years.
Precession, the axis wobble, takes roughly 23,000 years.
Together they change how much summer sunshine reaches the far north, where ice sheets grow and melt.
In 1976, deep-sea sediment cores confirmed this rhythm.
The nudges are small, but feedbacks amplify them.
Spreading ice reflects more sunlight, and colder oceans absorb more carbon dioxide.
Antarctic ice cores, going back about 800,000 years, show carbon dioxide at roughly 180 parts per million in glacial periods and about 280 in warm ones.
Ice-age Australia.
The Last Glacial Maximum, roughly 26,000 to 19,000 years ago, was the coldest part of the last glacial period.
Ice sheets up to about 3 kilometres thick covered Canada, the northern United States and much of northern Europe.
Global temperatures were around 6 degrees Celsius colder than before the industrial era, though figures vary.
Woolly mammoths and cave lions roamed Europe's cold steppes.
Australia had no large ice sheets, but it was colder, drier and windier, and desert dunes expanded.
Glaciers carved Tasmania's highlands, including Cradle Mountain's lakes, and small glaciers formed near Mount Kosciuszko.
Willandra Lakes, including Lake Mungo, held water at various times.
Aboriginal people had already lived here for tens of thousands of years and adapted to these harsh conditions.
Lower seas, Sahul.
At the Last Glacial Maximum, so much water was locked up in ice that global sea levels were roughly 120 metres lower than today.
Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania formed a single landmass scientists call Sahul.
Bass Strait was a broad plain that could be walked across, and a land bridge joined Cape York to New Guinea.
A similar landmass, Sunda, joined Indonesian islands to Asia.
As the ice melted, seas rose, at times by more than a metre per century.
Tasmania was cut off roughly 12,000 years ago and New Guinea roughly 8,000 years ago, though estimates vary.
Seas reached near present levels about 7,000 years ago.
Some researchers suggest certain Aboriginal oral traditions may preserve memories of rising seas, an idea taken seriously but still debated.
What it means for us.
A modest change in sunlight, amplified by ice and carbon dioxide feedbacks, was enough to shift global temperatures by several degrees and sea levels by over 100 metres.
Today, carbon dioxide has risen from about 280 parts per million before industry to well over 400, higher than at any time in the ice-core record and far faster than natural glacial cycles.
On orbital grounds alone, scientists expect the next glacial period is many tens of thousands of years away, and human emissions may delay it further.
The coastlines we know, and the Aboriginal history written into them, are a reminder that the map is never permanent.
The key idea: Technically we live in an ice age, in a warm interglacial period that began about 11,700 years ago.
Part two. Glaciers: rivers of ice.
Glaciers look frozen in place, but they flow, grind and carve like slow-motion rivers.
They shaped many of the world's most beautiful landscapes, including some in Tasmania.
Ice that moves.
Stand beside a glacier in New Zealand or Alaska and you will hear it creak, groan and sometimes crack like a gunshot, because it is moving.
A glacier is a large body of ice that forms on land and flows downhill or outward under its own weight.
Most move perhaps tens of centimetres to a few metres a day, though some outlet glaciers in Greenland and Antarctica race along at many kilometres a year.
Glaciers and ice sheets together hold most of the planet's fresh water, around two thirds by common estimates.
Glaciers exist on every continent except mainland Australia, from tropical peaks in South America and Africa to the polar regions.
From snow to flowing ice.
Every glacier begins as snow.
Where more falls in winter than melts in summer, it builds up year after year.
As new layers pile on, older snow is compressed into rounded grains called firn.
Over years to centuries the firn is squeezed until the air spaces close off as tiny bubbles and it becomes solid glacier ice.
Thick ice absorbs red light, which is why deep crevasses glow blue, and the trapped bubbles preserve samples of ancient air.
Under enough pressure, solid ice behaves a little like stiff toffee.
Its crystals slowly deform and slide past one another, and many glaciers also slide on meltwater at their base.
The brittle surface cracks into crevasses, which can be tens of metres deep and hidden under snow bridges.
Nature's bulldozers.
As a glacier moves, it plucks rocks from its bed and drags them along like sandpaper.
A river usually cuts a narrow V-shaped valley, but a glacier widens and deepens it into a broad U with steep walls.
At the head of a glacier, ice gouges a bowl-shaped hollow called a cirque, which often holds a lake after the ice melts.
Where several cirques eat into a mountain from different sides, they leave a sharp pyramid peak, as with the Matterhorn in the Alps.
When glaciers carve valleys below sea level and the ice later retreats, the sea floods in, creating fjords like those of Norway and Fiordland in New Zealand.
What glaciers leave behind.
Glaciers are messy.
Everything they carry, from fine rock flour to boulders the size of houses, is dumped where the ice melts.
Ridges of this debris are called moraines, and they mark the sides and furthest reach of old glaciers.
Huge lone boulders sitting far from any matching rock are glacial erratics.
In the 1800s, scientists such as Louis Agassiz used clues like these to argue that much of Europe had once been buried under ice, an idea that was startling at the time.
Meltwater is milky with fine rock flour, which is why glacier-fed lakes often glow turquoise, as at Lake Tekapo in New Zealand and Lake Louise in Canada.
Tasmania and a warming world.
Mainland Australia has no glaciers today, and saw only small ones in the Snowy Mountains during the last ice age.
Tasmania tells a different story.
Ice caps and glaciers once covered parts of the Central Highlands and West Coast ranges.
Dove Lake, beneath Cradle Mountain, sits in a basin carved by ice, and Lake St Clair, Australia's deepest freshwater lake, was also shaped by glaciers.
Heard Island, an Australian territory in the Southern Ocean, still has active glaciers.
Worldwide, most mountain glaciers are losing ice, linked to rising temperatures.
Their meltwater feeds rivers that supply many millions of people, and shrinking glaciers may mean lower summer flows.
In 2019 Iceland held a memorial for Okjokull, a glacier that had lost so much ice it was no longer considered one.
The key idea: A glacier is a large mass of ice that flows downhill under its own weight.
Part three. When the Sahara was green.
Ten thousand years ago, people fished, swam and herded cattle across land that is now the world's largest hot desert.
A wobble in Earth's orbit explains how.
Hippos in the desert.
The Sahara covers around nine million square kilometres of North Africa, larger than Australia, and much of it gets almost no rain.
Yet clues to a different past are scattered across it.
Rock paintings and engravings at places like Tassili n'Ajjer in Algeria show giraffes, elephants, rhinoceroses, hippopotamuses and herds of cattle.
Fossilised crocodile and fish bones lie in bare sand, and ancient shorelines mark vanished lakes.
Mega-Lake Chad once covered hundreds of thousands of square kilometres.
Scientists call this wetter time the African Humid Period, lasting roughly from 15,000 to 5,000 years ago.
In 1933 explorer László Almásy found the Cave of Swimmers in Egypt's Gilf Kebir, whose figures appear to swim, though some researchers think they may be spiritual rather than literal.
The orbital wobble.
The main driver was astronomical.
Earth's axis slowly wobbles, like a spinning top, in a cycle of roughly 20,000 to 26,000 years called precession.
This changes the time of year when Earth is closest to the Sun.
Around 10,000 years ago the Northern Hemisphere was closest during its summer, so North Africa received noticeably more summer sunshine than today.
Stronger heating over the land drew the West African monsoon much further north, carrying rain deep into what is now desert.
Feedbacks amplified the change: plants and lakes darkened the landscape and recycled moisture into the air, helping the rains persist.
The opposite process eventually dried the region out.
People of the green Sahara.
People moved into the Sahara as it greened.
At Gobero, in Niger, archaeologists working from 2000 onwards uncovered graves of communities who lived beside an ancient lake.
Their remains lay with bone harpoons, fish hooks and pottery, along with bones of fish, turtles and crocodiles.
One moving burial held a woman and two children, apparently laid to rest together.
Across the region people made some of the world's early pottery and, later, took up cattle herding as conditions became drier and less predictable.
Rock art shows people with herds and dogs.
This was not a single culture but many groups, adapting over thousands of years to a landscape that kept changing around them.
Drying out.
As Earth's orbit continued its slow cycle, summer sunshine in North Africa weakened and the monsoon retreated south.
The lakes shrank, the grasslands thinned and the Sahara became desert again around 5,000 years ago.
Scientists still debate how quickly.
Ocean sediments, which record dust blown off Africa, suggest a fairly abrupt shift over a few centuries.
Lake and pollen records suggest a more gradual drying that varied by place.
The people there had to adapt, and many appear to have moved towards more reliable water, including the Nile Valley.
Some archaeologists suggest this migration played a part in the rise of early Egyptian civilisation, though that link remains a hypothesis.
A desert that breathes.
The green period was not unique.
Sediment records show the Sahara has swung between desert and grassland many times over hundreds of thousands of years, roughly in step with the precession cycle.
These green corridors may have opened routes for animals and early humans to move out of Africa.
Even as a desert, the Sahara shapes the planet.
Winds lift hundreds of millions of tonnes of dust each year and carry it across the Atlantic.
Much comes from the Bodele Depression in Chad, the dried bed of the old mega-lake.
Satellite studies suggest this dust delivers phosphorus and other nutrients to the Amazon rainforest, helping fertilise one of Earth's richest ecosystems.
The key idea: Rock art, fossils and ancient shorelines show the Sahara once had lakes, grasslands and large animals.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why do geologists say we are still in an ice age?
Answer. Ice sheets still cover Antarctica and Greenland.
Question two. What makes a glacier move?
Answer. Its own weight pulling it downhill.
Question three. Which of these is evidence that the Sahara was once green?
Answer. Rock art showing hippos and cattle.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
